Patch Set 1: Ok-To-Test+1

User approved, CI ok to start

Patch Set 1: Verified+1

Build Successful 

https://jenkins.openbmc.org/job/ci-repository/113430/ : SUCCESS

Abandoned

Abandoning for now given the push-back.  I plan to attempt to build and fix issues out of tree/offline in the meantime.
Why are we enabling random compiler flags in random repositories??  If this is something useful, shouldn't we do this in the CI scripts?

> Why are we enabling random compiler flags 

I'm not sure what makes flags random, so I don't know how to respond.

> in random repositories

Reading between the lines a little here, but I assume there is a desire for all the projects to have the exact same clang-tidy configuration?

> shouldn't we do this in the CI scripts?

In general I will always support more static analysis but I don't think a one-size-fits-all approach is important.

> I'm not sure what makes flags random, so I don't know how to respond.

There are a huge set of compile flags here, of which only 5 are discussed in the commit message.  They just seem like a random collection to anyone else.  For example:

        '-Wno-c++20-extensions',
        '-Wno-c++23-extensions',

Why do we need to disable warnings for C++23 extensions when we're using C++23?

If we have to specify this many things to make something work, I see it as being low value.  You mentioned 5 flags that are "especially valuable".  Why not enable those rather than `-Weverything`?

> Reading between the lines a little here, but I assume there is a desire for all the projects to have the exact same clang-tidy configuration?

Yes, 100%.  We've spent way too much time unraveling compiler flags and boost #defines that snuck their way into meson.build files already.  I'm tired of it.  In my opinion, if a repository has to specify compile flags in a meson.build in order for their repository to work like everyone else's, something is wrong.

> In general I will always support more static analysis but I don't think a one-size-fits-all approach is important.

I think we should treat this just like clang-tidy flags: no repository should be a special snowflake.  If you think there is a valuable flag, let's get it enabled a project level (with potentially a way to turn it off for repositories that aren't "ready") so we can have the debate there.  Having one repository do one thing and another repository do another is more technical debt than technical benefit, in my mind.

Lets start by documenting where these came from.  Unless we happened to pick the exact same option order to ignore, i'm assuming these came from bmcweb, which has run -Weverything for a while.

https://github.com/openbmc/bmcweb/blob/1060065e881844d3adbd23d0e6c14b855bee4726/meson.build#L79

FWIW, the clang maintainers don't recommend running -Weverything because it causes new-issues with -Werror every release.  Within a day or two of the clang release I have to run a build and put up a commit like:
https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/bmcweb/+/80867

Or a commit to go clean up all the warnings for -Werror ahead of clang getting enabled.  Do you guys as maintainers know that's what this entails?

FWIW, when I did this in bmcweb 23a21a1cbed23ace4174664950e595df961e9e69 (5 years ago), I intended this to be temporary, and I wanted to make up an explicit list of warnings to enable and propose in openbmc-build-scripts as things every repo should pass.  Of course... I never got there, but that was the goal.  Every clang release I've toyed with removing -Weverything.  I've ended up working around it thusfar, but it's a non-trivial amount of work.  object mapper is probably less work due to it being a lot less code, but it's still work that happens on a deadline.

> Why do we need to disable warnings for C++23 extensions when we're using C++23?

Because bmcweb was on c++20 when I enabled these.  https://github.com/openbmc/bmcweb/commit/27f5ecf750efa7ef437d3a078e766a84265adf67

We're wrong to still have that in the list, so might as well clean that up:
https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/bmcweb/+/82703

> in order for their repository to work like everyone else's,

This isn't really true.  Most of the build tree still won't compile with clang as-is.  In this case of clang, I would like to see us consolidate the warnings (likely with the exception of -Weverything) but I don't think taking this patch as it stands is outright wrong.

> I think we should treat this just like clang-tidy flags: no repository should be a special snowflake.

While I agree with this position in general, it forgets the reality that we have lots of maintainers that don't integrate new checks and changes over time, and we have a lot of code written against a lot of different quality standards.  The majority of the repos still aren't tidy enabled, so these checks are largely moot.  I would much rather have the checks enabled in the places that we do work in because as a maintainer it saves me time to, for example, not have to point out that people check before they dereferenced their optional (bugprone-unchecked-optional-access).  In almost every case where the code had that in bmcweb, that was a crash we avoided on untrusted user data, but the check would be difficult to turn on for the whole project.  There are plenty of examples where we've also enabled warnings that are counter productive, and we fix just to keep from needing to update the list of warnings.  That subtlety makes it hard to come up with a one size fits all approach to this.

Overal:
Enabling phosphor-object manager to build with clang, I'm in support, and I suspect the rest of this series is only making improvements on things that clang found to be wrong.

Enabling -Weverything..... I'd be good to have a discussion on how that's maintained, and if there's a better option there (fixed clang-specific warning list in openbmc-build-scripts) that doesn't cause a bunch of distributed work for everyone now that people besides me care about -Weverything.  I would really like to synchronize with others on it, and if copy/paste is the only way to do that, so be it, but I suspect something like openbmc-build-scripts would end up being better.

> of which only 5 are discussed in the commit message.

They are all discussed in the commit message - they are either in the group of not helpful or the group of one of the five listed that are helpful but don't pass the code as is.

> Why do we need to disable warnings for C++23 extensions when we're using C++23?

That's not how these options work.  -Wc++26-extensions means 'complain about use of c++26' so I'm turning that off so we can use c++26.

> You mentioned 5 flags that are "especially valuable". Why not enable those rather than -Weverything?

I mentioned 5 that are helpful that don't pass.  There are more that are helpful that do pass.

> We've spent way too much time unraveling compiler flags and boost #defines that snuck their way into meson.build files already. I'm tired of it.

Who spent time doing what exactly?  I don't anticipate causing work for anyone other that myself or maybe Matt.

> Lets start by documenting where these came from

Yes, they came from bmcweb.

> Do you guys as maintainers know that's what this entails?

Yes, I was aware I was taking that on (or we can work on it together).
